screens.title: What is a physical base backup?
screens.narratorSegment: A physical base backup is a complete copy of the PostgreSQL data directory, PGDATA, taken at a specific point in time. It is not a logical export of tables; it is the raw files that the server uses. This matters because Point-in-Time Recovery depends on a base backup plus the WAL segments produced after that snapshot. The base backup provides the disk image to which WAL records can be applied. A practical example: when you run pg_basebackup in plain format, you receive a directory structure identical to the live PGDATA, including the data files and a base. backup marker. A common misconception is to treat a base backup as sufficient by itself for PITR; it is only the starting point. If the WAL segments generated during the backup are not preserved or included, recovery may stop early. The core takeaway is that a base backup and a continuous WAL archive together create an unbroken recovery chain. Consider how you would verify a base backup: list the destination contents, confirm a base. backup file exists, and inspect pg_wal to ensure WAL segments are present. How will you ensure your backups include the necessary WALs?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › What is a physical base backup?
Definition
A complete copy of PGDATA at a known point; used as the anchor for applying WALs during recovery.
Why it matters
It provides the physical files onto which WAL records are applied for Point-in-Time Recovery.
Common misconception
A base backup alone is sometimes treated as sufficient; without the WAL stream or archived WALs produced during the backup, PITR may not be possible.
Key check
Verify presence of base.backup and WAL files in pg_wal or tar contents after the run.
Analogy
Think of a base backup as taking a photograph of a server’s disk layout at a moment; WALs are the film negatives that record changes after the photo. You need both to recreate the full sequence of states.
Concrete example
pg_basebackup -h localhost -U postgres -D /mnt/pg_backups/base_backup_20210930_120000 -P
This creates a plain-format copy of PGDATA in the destination directory. Inspect the directory for base.backup and pg_wal.
Key Takeaway

Base backups plus preserved WAL segments equal a usable PITR starting point; without WALs the backup is incomplete.

screens.title: Server prerequisites for pg_basebackup
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can run pg_basebackup, the server must permit replication connections and produce the WAL detail required by streaming. Practically this means two things: first, set wal_level to replica so the server writes the additional information needed for streaming WAL segments. Second, configure pg_hba. conf to permit the backup client to connect as a replication user. A simple pg_hba. conf line looks like host replication postgres 192.168.1.0/24 md5 and must match the backup host’s IP. After editing pg_hba. conf you must reload the server configuration so the new rule takes effect. Also check max_wal_senders; if you intend to use -X stream, the server must have enough wal sender slots for the backup connection and any other replication clients. A misconception is to change only the client command; if wal_level remains minimal the server will not stream WALs. As a concrete example, set wal_level = replica in postgresql. conf, add the replication host to pg_hba. conf, reload Postgres, and then run pg_basebackup. Before you start, validate connectivity with a replication-capable user to avoid authentication failures during the backup. Server prerequisites for pg_basebackup means ensure wal_level=replica, appropriate pg_hba.replication entries, and sufficient max_wal_senders before running pg_basebackup with wal streaming.. In practical terms, wal_level, max_wal_senders and pg_hba.conf entries for replication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Server prerequisites
Key server settings
These settings enable replication protocol access and WAL streaming.
wal_level = replica
Enables required WAL detail for streaming and archiving.
max_wal_senders
Provide enough senders for -X stream backups and other replication clients.
pg_hba.conf entry
Add host replication USER ADDR METHOD and reload Postgres to apply changes.
Command example (pg_hba.conf)
# pg_hba.conf
host    replication     postgres        192.168.1.0/24          md5
After editing, reload with pg_ctl reload or the system service equivalent so the server accepts replication connections immediately.
Misconception

Editing only the client command without setting wal_level to replica will not enable streaming WAL delivery; the server must be configured.

screens.title: pg_hba.conf and reloading configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring pg_hba. conf is a small edit with a big effect. To permit pg_basebackup to connect, add a replication-type line with the backup user and the source IP or CIDR for the backup host. For example, host replication postgres 192.168.1.0/24 md5 grants the postgres user replication access from that network using password authentication. After you change pg_hba. conf, you must reload the PostgreSQL configuration; this applies the new access rules without restarting the server. Use pg_ctl reload or the system service reload command. A common error is forgetting to reload, which leads to authentication failures even when the file has the correct entry. Another frequent mistake is overly permissive pg_hba. conf entries that expose replication access; prefer precise addresses and dedicated replication users where possible. In practice, test the replication connection with a simple psql connection that requests replication capability before launching the full pg_basebackup to reduce wasted time and unexpected failures. pg_hba.conf and reloading configuration means add a host replication entry for the backup user in pg_hba.conf and reload postgres to permit pg_basebackup connections.. In practical terms, allowing replication connections and applying changes safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Edit, then reload
Add a host replication line, save, and reload to apply without restart.
Example pg_hba.conf line
host    replication     postgres        192.168.1.0/24          md5
Reload example: pg_ctl reload or sudo systemctl reload postgresql@12-main depending on your platform.
Process checklist
  • Back up current pg_hba.conf before editing.
  • Add precise host/CIDR, avoid 0.0.0.0/0 for replication.
  • Reload Postgres to apply the change immediately.
  • Test a replication-capable connection before running pg_basebackup.
Common mistake

Forgetting to reload after changing pg_hba.conf causes confusing authentication errors during backup attempts.

screens.title: Simple plain-format pg_basebackup command
screens.narratorSegment: The simplest invocation of pg_basebackup creates a plain-format directory structure identical to PGDATA. A practical, recommended pattern is to create a timestamped destination so you avoid overwriting previous backups. For example, running pg_basebackup -h localhost -U postgres -D /mnt/pg_backups/base_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S) -P will connect over the replication protocol, create the destination directory if it does not exist, and show progress. Important details: the destination must be empty or absent because pg_basebackup creates and populates it. The connecting user requires REPLICATION privilege and the destination must be writable by the process running pg_basebackup. A common misconception is that pg_basebackup can append to an existing backup; it cannot. If you need an archive, use tar format instead. When you run the plain-format command with -X stream, WAL segments are included in the resulting pg_wal directory. After the run, inspect base. backup and pg_wal to validate the backup content. How will you ensure destinations are uniquely named in your environment? Simple plain-format pg_basebackup command means a plain-format base backup produces a directory identical to pgdata; ensure a unique, empty destination and correct permissions.. In practical terms, run a direct copy of pgdata that can be used for immediate restore. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Plain-format pg_basebackup
Command walkthrough
Use a timestamped directory and show progress.
pg_basebackup -h localhost -U postgres -D /mnt/pg_backups/base_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S) -P
Notes: destination must be empty or not exist; creating a timestamp avoids accidental overwrites. The user needs REPLICATION privilege.
Explanation of flags

  • -U user: the connecting user with REPLICATION privilege.
  • -D destination: directory to create and populate.
  • -P: show progress during the backup.
Key Takeaway

Plain format is ready-to-restore into PGDATA; always use a unique destination and check permissions beforehand.

screens.title: Plain vs Tar formats
screens.narratorSegment: pg_basebackup supports two common output formats: the plain directory format and the tar archive format. The plain format produces a directory structure identical to PGDATA, which is convenient when you plan to restore directly into a data directory or create a standby by copying files. Tar format creates a single archive file, which can be easier to transfer, compress, or store. For example, you might prefer tar when moving backups between datacenters or when storing them in object storage. A common mistake is choosing tar without planning how to extract and place files for restore; tar archives still contain the same base. backup and pg_wal files, but restoration requires careful extraction into an empty PGDATA destination. Use -F tar and optionally --compress for tar format. In contrast, plain format is ideal for immediate file-based restores on a host with matching filesystem layout. Consider your recovery process: if you need portability, choose tar; if you need immediate directory-level restore, choose plain. Which format fits your operational restore runbook? Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Plain vs Tar formats
Plain (default)
Creates directory structure identical to PGDATA for direct restore.
  • Restore: copy files into PGDATA and start server.
  • Use when you have the same filesystem layout and want immediate file-level access.
Tar (-F tar)
Produces a single tar archive file, which is convenient for transport and compression.
  • Good for moving backups between sites or storing in object storage.

pg_basebackup -h localhost -U postgres -D /mnt/pg_backups/base_backup_20210930.tar -F tar -P

screens.title: Including WAL files with pg_basebackup
screens.narratorSegment: Including WAL segments created during a base backup is essential for producing a self-consistent backup suitable for PITR. pg_basebackup offers three main choices: -X stream streams WAL segments from the server while the backup runs and includes them in the backup bundle. This is the most common and recommended approach because it ensures no WAL gap exists between the base backup and subsequent WALs. -X fetch requests the required WAL files after the base backup completes by fetching from the server’s archive or file locations; it can be slower and requires fewer concurrent sender slots. -X none omits WAL files entirely; this is only appropriate if you already have a reliable, continuous WAL archiving mechanism and are certain the missing segments are archived elsewhere. A common misconception is to rely solely on archive_mode without including WALs during the base backup; if the small window of WALs produced during the backup was not archived quickly enough, the archive may miss segments needed for PITR. Choose -X stream when you want the backup to be self-contained and immediate for recovery. Including WAL files with pg_basebackup means -x stream includes wals while backing up; -x fetch retrieves them afterwards; -x none includes no wals and should be used only with reliable external archiving.. In practical terms, -x stream, -x fetch, and -x none explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Including WAL files
WAL options
Choose how pg_basebackup includes the WAL segments required for recovery.
-X stream
Streams WAL segments from the server while the backup runs and places them in the backup. Recommended for a self-contained PITR starting point.
-X fetch
Fetches required WAL files after the backup completes. Useful when sender slots are limited but may be slower.
-X none
No WALs included. Use only if you have a reliable external WAL archive and are confident nothing will be missing.
Example: stream
pg_basebackup -h localhost -U postgres -D /mnt/pg_backups/base_backup_stream -P -X stream
Why stream

Streaming ensures WALs produced during the backup are captured immediately, preventing gaps in the recovery chain.

screens.title: The role of checkpoints during a base backup
screens.narratorSegment: A checkpoint is when PostgreSQL flushes dirty data pages to disk and records a stable point in the WAL. During a pg_basebackup run the server performs and completes a checkpoint so the backup starts from a known consistent disk state. This matters because without a checkpoint the on-disk files might reflect a mix of states that cannot be recovered simply by applying WALs. pg_basebackup waits for that checkpoint, ensuring the backup includes the disk contents aligned with a checkpoint record. A concrete example: when a long-running write-heavy workload exists, the checkpoint ensures dirty pages are on disk so the base backup has a consistent base to which WALs can be applied. A common misconception is that streaming WALs alone make checkpoints unnecessary; they do not. The checkpoint plus WALs together guarantee the base backup is consistent and recoverable. Reflect on how long checkpoints take in your environment and plan backup windows so checkpoints do not cause unacceptable input and output spikes. The role of checkpoints during a base backup means pg_basebackup waits for a checkpoint to guarantee the on-disk state is consistent; wals then replay from that checkpoint forward.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: There are several practical pitfalls when performing physical base backups. First, insufficient disk space is a frequent cause of failure. Physical backups can be very large, so ensure the destination has ample free space before starting. Second, permissions matter: the postgres user or the user running pg_basebackup must own and write to the destination. Third, network instability can interrupt remote backups and cause failed or partial backups. Fourth, overwriting existing backups is risky—always use timestamped directories or filenames to keep versions separate. Fifth, not testing backups makes them effectively useless; periodically restore to a separate environment to verify recoverability. Finally, excluding WALs during the base backup without a dependable external archive can break the recovery chain. A common misconception is assuming a successful run means restore will succeed; testing is the only way to confirm. For safety, script destination creation with chown and verify disk space before each run, and use -X stream to include WALs when possible. Common pitfalls and safety notes means verify disk space, permissions, network stability, unique destinations, and test restores; include wals to avoid recovery gaps.. screens.title: Best practices for PITR and recovery chains
screens.narratorSegment: To maintain a reliable Point-in-Time Recovery capability, follow a few consistent best practices. First, prefer pg_basebackup with -X stream so the WAL segments produced during the backup are captured and included, avoiding small gaps in the recovery chain. Second, always use unique timestamped destination directories or filenames to prevent accidental overwrites of previous valid backups. Third, ensure archive_mode and archive_command are configured and tested so WALs are archived continuously; even with streaming, a separate archive gives you redundancy. Fourth, plan for disk space and rotate or expire old backups according to your retention policy. Fifth, test restores regularly in an isolated environment to validate the entire process, not just backup creation. A common scenario: running pg_basebackup without -X stream while archive_mode is enabled can still fail PITR if some WALs produced during the backup were not archived quickly enough. The safest approach is -X stream plus monitored archive configuration so your base backup and WAL archive form an unbroken recovery chain. Best practices for PITR and recovery chains means combine -x stream with reliable wal archiving, timestamped destinations, and regular restore testing to ensure recoverable backups.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to produce a consistent physical base backup of a running PostgreSQL 12 cluster using the pg_basebackup utility. A base backup is the starting point for Point-in-Time Recovery and must capture a consistent snapshot of PGDATA plus the WAL segments needed to complete recovery. We’ll practice the commands that create plain directory backups and tar archives, and explain the critical options for including WAL segments during the backup so the chain is unbroken. You’ll also see which server settings must be enabled for replication connections and why a checkpoint is important while the backup runs. As you follow along, notice the difference between a plain-format directory that can be restored directly and a tar-format archive that’s easier to move or compress. The practical examples include creating a timestamped destination directory, ensuring file ownership, and using -X stream to include WAL segments. By the end of this module you will understand the commands to run, the configuration prerequisites to set, and the common pitfalls to avoid so a base backup remains useful for PITR. Consider how you might test one of these backups in a separate environment.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to execute pg_basebackup to create a consistent physical base backup, choose the appropriate output format, and include WAL segments so the backup supports PITR. You will understand the server-side prerequisites such as setting wal_level to replica and configuring pg_hba. conf to allow replication connections, and why a checkpoint is performed and awaited by the backup process. You will also be able to inspect a backup directory or tar archive to verify the presence of a base. backup file and pg_wal content, and perform basic troubleshooting when authentication or permissions prevent the backup from succeeding. Finally, you will adopt a few best practices: use timestamped unique destinations, verify destination ownership and space before the run, and test restores periodically. These skills combine configuration, command execution, validation, and operational safety so your backups are reliable and restorable when needed.

This continuation focuses on configuration, checkpoints, and safety checks you must perform before and after running a base backup. You will learn to set wal_level to replica and to add a replication line in pg_hba. conf so the backup client can connect. You will practice reloading Postgres configuration after edits and understand why the server performs a checkpoint during a base backup: it guarantees a known consistent point and flushes dirty pages to disk. You will learn to check for sufficient disk space, correct destination ownership, and stable network connectivity. Finally, we will cover common pitfalls such as overwriting previous backups and the risk of missing WAL segments when -X options are not used. Practicing these checks prevents common failures and ensures the base backup can form the anchor for a PITR strategy.

A physical base backup is a complete copy of the PostgreSQL data directory, PGDATA, taken at a specific point in time. It is not a logical export of tables; it is the raw files that the server uses. This matters because Point-in-Time Recovery depends on a base backup plus the WAL segments produced after that snapshot. The base backup provides the disk image to which WAL records can be applied. A practical example: when you run pg_basebackup in plain format, you receive a directory structure identical to the live PGDATA, including the data files and a base. backup marker. A common misconception is to treat a base backup as sufficient by itself for PITR; it is only the starting point. If the WAL segments generated during the backup are not preserved or included, recovery may stop early. The core takeaway is that a base backup and a continuous WAL archive together create an unbroken recovery chain. Consider how you would verify a base backup: list the destination contents, confirm a base. backup file exists, and inspect pg_wal to ensure WAL segments are present. How will you ensure your backups include the necessary WALs?

Before you can run pg_basebackup, the server must permit replication connections and produce the WAL detail required by streaming. Practically this means two things: first, set wal_level to replica so the server writes the additional information needed for streaming WAL segments. Second, configure pg_hba. conf to permit the backup client to connect as a replication user. A simple pg_hba. conf line looks like host replication postgres 192.168.1.0/24 md5 and must match the backup host’s IP. After editing pg_hba. conf you must reload the server configuration so the new rule takes effect. Also check max_wal_senders; if you intend to use -X stream, the server must have enough wal sender slots for the backup connection and any other replication clients. A misconception is to change only the client command; if wal_level remains minimal the server will not stream WALs. As a concrete example, set wal_level = replica in postgresql. conf, add the replication host to pg_hba. conf, reload Postgres, and then run pg_basebackup. Including WAL segments created during a base backup is essential for producing a self-consistent backup suitable for PITR. pg_basebackup offers three main choices: -X stream streams WAL segments from the server while the backup runs and includes them in the backup bundle. There are several practical pitfalls when performing physical base backups. First, insufficient disk space is a frequent cause of failure. Physical backups can be very large, so ensure the destination has ample free space before starting. Second, permissions matter: the postgres user or the user running pg_basebackup must own and write to the destination. Third, network instability can interrupt remote backups and cause failed or partial backups. Fourth, overwriting existing backups is risky—always use timestamped directories or filenames to keep versions separate. Fifth, not testing backups makes them effectively useless; periodically restore to a separate environment to verify recoverability. Finally, excluding WALs during the base backup without a dependable external archive can break the recovery chain. A common misconception is assuming a successful run means restore will succeed; testing is the only way to confirm.
